title: Vanity of vanities (Ecclesiastes 1:1–11)
hookLine: the Preacher says everything is breath, vapor, fleeting

lines: THE SUN, THE WIND, THE RIVERS.
cards: Proverbs ends with a capable woman whose works praise her in the gates. Turn one page, and a very different voice clears its throat. He calls himself the Preacher.

He's had everything: wealth, building projects, gardens, pleasure, learning. And his first words are a shrug that echoes through the whole book. The sun comes up, goes down, and hurries around to rise again.
The wind blows south, swings north, around and around. Every river runs into the sea, and the sea is never full. One generation goes, another comes, and the earth just stays.

teach.h: NOT A MIRROR: HEVEL MEANS BREATH.
teach.b: In the King James Bible the book opens: "Vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher, vanity of vanities; all is vanity." Vanity, to us, means staring in a mirror. That's not it.
The Hebrew word is hevel, and it means breath. Vapor. The puff of mist on a cold morning, there and gone.
Vanity of vanities is a Hebrew way of saying the most of something, like king of kings.
So: breath of breaths. Everything is breath. Hevel shows up again and again in this short book.
And a quiet echo: hevel is also the name Abel, the second son in Genesis, whose life was over almost before it began. Now, what does the Preacher mean? Readers hear different things.

Some hear meaningless, and the book can feel bleak. Others hear fleeting: not worthless, just impossible to hold, like trying to grab your own breath. Others hear mystery: things too thin to see through.
The Preacher himself, in Hebrew Qohelet, seems to mean all of these at different moments.

Christian readers have taken him more than one way: as a warning against chasing what won't last, as an honest companion for people in grief, as a voice that says out loud what people sometimes think and don't say.
Strangely, the book doesn't end in despair. It keeps returning to bread, work, friendship and joy as gifts to enjoy while you have them. Breath is fleeting.
It's also what keeps you alive.

how: Christians read Ecclesiastes in personal study and in times of grief, and it is sometimes preached as a counterweight to ambition; in Jewish practice the book is read in the synagogue during the festival of Sukkot.

o: pride in your looks, like staring in a mirror
a sin that God punishes in the Preacher's book
breath, vapor, a puff of mist there and gone

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.

s: vanity in Ecclesiastes means being proud of your looks
the Hebrew hevel means breath or vapor: fleeting, impossible to hold.
Abel's name in Hebrew is the same word, hevel
the brother whose life was over almost before it began carries the name breath.
it keeps returning to bread, work, friendship and joy as gifts to enjoy while you can.

games.q: you've had everything: wealth, gardens, learning, pleasure. what's the first thing you say about it all?
games.why: the Preacher's first words: "vanity of vanities; all is vanity": breath of breaths. the man who had it all opens with how little of it can be held.

practice: If there's a cold window nearby, breathe on it and watch the mist appear and fade; if not, breathe out slowly and feel each breath go, and the next one come anyway.
Then bring to mind one thing you've been gripping tightly, a plan, a worry, an achievement, and let it be breath for a moment: not worthless, just not yours to hold forever.

wordCard.voice: Hevel. Breath, vapor, a puff of mist. The King James Bible says vanity; the Preacher means everything under the sun is fleeting.

orig.note: Hebrew: breath, vapor. also the name of Abel, Adam and Eve's second son.

carryVoice: Your line: all is breath. The Preacher has only just begun. Day four hundred fifty-four, done.
